title: Search development plan
text:
Goal: PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science queries for RDS-Review, built from the Research Protocol’s PCC table and tested against the sources Chawinga and Zinn (2019) included.
Outcome: one query, run in all three databases: a form of share within five words of data in the title, leaving out titles that name blockchain, smart contracts, the Internet of Things, vehicular networks, edge computing or cloud computing, for 2015 to 2025 in English and French. The Term evidence section of notebook 00 records how it was chosen, and the search strategy page gives each database’s string.
Location: the work lives in the RDS-Review repo, in analysis/00_search-development/. Files the APIs and the local model produce go in data/raw/search-development/; files notebook 00 builds go in data/processed/search-development/. The review’s search exports come later, from each database’s own interface, and go in data/raw/search_exports/ as that folder’s README sets out. The work runs in three places:
Reproducibility: every file comes from code in the repo, except one judgment, recorded so it can be checked: the comparison of their criteria with the RDS-Review criteria, with page references, in comparison.csv. The choices among the measured queries are recorded, with their reasons, in log.md.
The reference set script reads the full text of Chawinga and Zinn (2019) through Elsevier’s Article Retrieval API, which needs an Elsevier API key with full-text entitlement for the journal; it writes only bibliographic details and citation locations, never the paper’s text. The coding and the assignment of indexing terms are made by a local model, pinned to one version, with fixed prompts and settings, so anyone with the same model can rerun them. The model is a GGUF file on Hugging Face, fixed by repository, revision and SHA-256, so the identical file stays available; the server is a llama.cpp build fixed by its image. The run records the model file, its checksum, the llama.cpp build and the settings with its output. The databases keep indexing new records, so a rerun of step 3 months later returns somewhat different counts; the committed outputs and log.md record what each search returned and when.

title: Search development plan
text:
Step 1. Comparability assessment

Inputs from Chawinga and Zinn, and their use:

Aim (abstract, p. 109): factors hampering data sharing at individual, institutional and international levels. Set against the RDS-Review Objective and questions.
Inclusion and exclusion criteria (section 3.1, p. 111): topic (data sharing), source type, empirical design, English, 2007 or later. Compared with the RDS-Review criteria in the method below.
Date range (section 3.1, p. 111; section 5.2, p. 115): 2007 to July 2018, so their set overlaps RDS-Review only for 2015 to July 2018.
Publications by year (Fig. 4, p. 113): 64 of their 105 sources date from 2007 to 2014 and 41 from 2015 to July 2018, the upper bounds for the development and test sets below.
Source types (section 3.1, p. 111; section 4, p. 112): they excluded conference papers, letters, editorials, book reviews, research notes and short communications. RDS-Review admits all source types, so their set can’t supply terms for these.
Search statements (section 3.2, p. 111): four statements. Matched against the reference set in the method below, to show how much of their set their own statements reach.
Reference list, Table 2, sections 4 and 5, and Figs. 3 to 5 (pp. 112–122): the paper gives no list of its 105 included sources. The reference set is reconstructed from the paper’s own evidence, below, and checked against its counts by type (section 4) and by year (Fig. 4).

Inputs from RDS-Review, and their use:

Objective and questions in the Research Protocol set the standard Chawinga and Zinn’s aim is compared against.
PCC table in the Research Protocol and Criteria in screening-guide.qmd supply the fields for coding Chawinga and Zinn’s included sources.
Factor themes and their terms in screening-guide.qmd supply the list for the Factors field.
Variables and exclusion codes in codebook.yml supply the data_origin, field, tier and source_type fields and the Reason values.
Date range, language limit and exclusions in the Research Protocol set the In scope criteria below.
Candidate terms table on the search strategy page supplies fallback terms for a Practice value with no development set sources, in step 2.

Reference set:

Select. The paper’s list of included sources was not published: the Crossref record lists no supplementary material, and the first author’s thesis, data deposits and profiles hold no list. The reference set script reads the paper’s full text and reference list from Elsevier and selects every reference the paper identifies as an included source, by three rules:

Table 2: references Table 2 names as sources for its themes, matched by first author and year, allowing a year either way only where the reference list holds no reference by that author with Table 2’s year.
Sections 4 and 5: references cited in the Results or the Discussion.
Section 4.3: section 4.3 lists the countries with one included publication each; a listed country that no reference selected by the first two rules names in its title is supplied by the reference, dated 2007 to 2018, whose title names it.

It writes reference_citations.csv, with every reference in the paper, where it is cited, its type and the rule that selected it, and reference_candidates.csv, with the selected references.
Look up. The lookups script checks each DOI against Crossref and OpenAlex, finds the PMID, and pulls the earliest publication date PubMed or Crossref gives (the year the paper cites where neither gives one), the title, the abstract (from PubMed, then OpenAlex, then Crossref, then the Scopus Abstract Retrieval API), the MeSH headings with their NLM scope notes, the author keywords and the OpenAlex keywords. It writes reference_lookups.csv and reference_indexing.csv. Where a reference has no DOI, or one neither Crossref nor OpenAlex knows, the lookups script searches OpenAlex by title, first author and year. A reference whose DOI or metadata can’t be verified is dropped and listed with the reason.
Size. The reference set script reports the size of the reference set against their 105, by type against their 83 journal articles, 10 theses, 8 reports and 4 books, and by year against Fig. 4.
Split. The reference set sources published 2007 to 2014 form the development set, which supplies terms in step 2. Those published 2015 or later form the test set, the latest dated September 2018, which measures coverage in step 3, so coverage is measured on sources the terms weren’t drawn from.

Local model: runs on a GPU server with ten 24 GB GPUs. scripts/launch_rds_llm.sh downloads the model’s GGUF file from Hugging Face at a fixed revision, checks its SHA-256, and starts a llama.cpp server on the GPUs it is given; a model too large for one GPU is split across several. Model files are stored in the folder MODELS_DIR names. scripts/README.md describes the launch script.

Model of record: Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (qwen3.5-122b, unsloth’s Q4_K_M build), on four GPUs. Its codes are reference_codes_qwen3.5-122b.csv, and each file of codes is named after the model that made it.
Smaller model: Qwen3.8-27B (qwen3.8-27b, unsloth’s UD-Q4_K_M build) runs on one 24 GB GPU, for anyone without the hardware for the larger one. Its codes, from the same prompt, schema and settings, are reference_codes_qwen3.8-27b.csv. Across the 102 sources, the two models agree on Practice for 86% of sources (Cohen’s kappa 0.74), data_origin 94% (0.80), field 86% (0.78), source_type 79% (0.71) and language 100%, and on whether a source reports a factor under each theme for 84% to 93% (kappa 0.63 to 0.84). The main differences: the larger model codes 9 sources both that the smaller codes sharing, and codes more factors, 3.0 per source against 2.3. The smaller model’s terms are less faithful to the source, with 10 codes whose term or passage the check could not find in the title or abstract, against 4 for the larger, 3 of those only a copied “Title:” label. Recorded terms become search terms in step 2, so the larger model is the one of record. For the assignment of the 637 indexing terms in step 2, the two models give the same value to 85% of terms (kappa 0.73) and place 90% under the same PCC part or none (0.81). All 5 reuse terms of the larger model are reuse for the smaller; of its 34 sharing terms, the smaller agrees on 29, and it leaves out MeSH Information Dissemination. Where they differ on factors, the larger model mostly places a term the smaller leaves as none, 22 of them under factors that facilitate. The smaller model’s assignments are term_assignments_qwen3.8-27b.csv.

Coding: local-model/coding.py sends each reference set source’s title and abstract from reference_lookups.csv to the local model with prompts/coding_prompt.md, which holds the definitions below, at temperature 0 with a fixed seed, thinking off and prompt caching off, and asks for a JSON answer. A source with no abstract is coded on its title, and its codes are marked so. Each code is checked against the prompt’s definitions, and against the title and abstract for its passage and term; a code that fails is kept and its problem recorded. Each coded value carries two things: the passage that supports it (the sentence from the title or abstract, or none where no sentence supports it), and the term in that passage that expresses the value, such as secondary use for reuse or unwilling to share for reluctance (none where the passage expresses the value without a distinct term).

Practice: sharing, reuse, both or neither.
data_origin:

research: data that researchers generate through procedures designed for a specific study, such as a trial, cohort, survey, experiment, interview study or fieldwork. Examples: trial measurements, survey responses, interview transcripts, sequencing data from study participants.
not-research-data: data that public health agencies, health services or clinicians generate while conducting surveillance, delivering services or treating patients, and that stay within those activities. Examples: electronic health records used for treatment, disease registries used for surveillance, insurance claims used for billing, notifiable disease reports used for outbreak response. A source on these data alone is out of scope with the exclusion code not-research-data.
reused: not-research-data that researchers later obtain and analyse. Examples: electronic health records analysed in an observational study, registry data used in an epidemiological study.
mixed: the source concerns research data and reused data, such as cohort data linked with health records.
unclear: the source names the data but does not state who generated them or why.

Factors: the factors the source reports, matched to the list below by meaning. For example, a source on researchers who withhold data for fear of losing credit reports reluctance. The list groups the factors under the five themes in screening-guide.qmd:

factors that obstruct: barriers, challenges, obstacles, reluctance, privacy
factors that facilitate: facilitators, enablers, incentives, motivation, infrastructure, repositories, interoperability
stakeholder perspectives: perceptions, attitudes, willingness
policies and what drive them: policies, mandates, open science, open data, open access, open research
mechanisms for implementation: governance, consent, licensing, ethics, stewardship, data management plans, data curation, digital curation
none if the source reports no factor on the list.

field: health, other or cross-disciplinary. tier: 1 for health, 2 otherwise.
source_type: empirical, review, policy-guidance, opinion or other.
Language: English, French or other, from the title and abstract.
Year: earliest of online or print publication, from reference_lookups.csv.
Reason: the codebook.yml exclusion code for each out-of-scope source, derived from the codes.
In scope: Practice not neither, data_origin not not-research-data, Factors not none, tier 1 or source_type review (the screening guide’s Criteria admit other fields only as a review or synthesis), Year 2015 to 2025, Language English or French.
Notebook 00 derives tier, Year, set, Reason, In scope and Eligible apart from year by these rules and writes them with the lookups to reference_sources.csv.
Eligible apart from year: every In scope criterion except Year and tier. Development set sources meeting it are the ones step 3 counts. tier stays out because the query carries no field terms and the tier decision happens at screening, so the query should retrieve sources from every field.

Method:

Count the reference set sources by each coded value, split by development and test set.
For each criterion Chawinga and Zinn set (topic, source type, empirical design, language, date; p. 111), enter a row in the comparison table with their criterion, the RDS-Review criterion for the same thing with its section heading, and the relation between them: match when both admit the same sources, overlap when each admits sources the other excludes, differ when they admit no sources in common. Where they set none (reuse, data_origin, factors, field, tier), the counts alone show what their set covers.
Run each of Chawinga and Zinn’s search statements against the titles and abstracts of the reference set sources, twice: with “research data sharing” as a phrase, and as separate words. Count the sources each reading matches.
Verdict. For each PCC part (sharing, reuse, each factor theme), state its coverage: covered when both the development set and the test set hold sources eligible apart from year coded for it; development only; test only; or not covered. The terms and coverage figures for a part are only as good as its verdict.

Output:

comparison.csv: the comparison table; notebook 00 shows it with the counts that bear on each criterion

title: Search development plan
text:
Step 2. Terms by PCC part
Step 2’s terms fed the first version of step 3, which chose terms by a yield rule. The measurements that replaced it start from the Candidate terms table and standard phrasings, and the query uses none of step 2’s terms. Its factor terms informed the screening guide.

PCC parts: the parts of the PCC table’s Concept row a term can sit under: sharing and reuse (the practice), and the five factor themes (the factors). Context gets no terms, since field terms would act as filters in the query and the field and tier decisions happen at screening. Population has no restriction and needs no terms.
Sources: every source in the development set.
Term types:

recorded: the terms in reference_codes_qwen3.5-122b.csv, taken from each source’s passages.
MeSH: the MeSH headings PubMed lists for the source (MEDLINE field MH), pulled by PMID for sources PubMed indexes.
author keyword: the keywords the authors list on the paper, from PubMed’s OT field, for sources PubMed indexes. Sources outside PubMed contribute no author keywords.
OpenAlex keyword: the keywords OpenAlex assigns to the work (its keywords field), pulled by DOI.

The lookups script in step 1 pulls all three into reference_indexing.csv.
Normalisation: all terms are lowercased. Variants that differ only by hyphen, plural or word ending merge into one term, written with truncation (reus*) where every word the truncation matches is a variant of the term, and as a list of variants joined with OR otherwise. MeSH headings keep NLM’s exact form.
Assignment: MeSH headings, author keywords and OpenAlex keywords attach to a whole source, so each is placed under a PCC part by meaning. local-model/indexing.py sends every distinct term in reference_indexing.csv, one term at a time, MeSH headings with their NLM scope notes, to the local model with prompts/indexing_prompt.md, at temperature 0 with a fixed seed, thinking and prompt caching off, with the answer held to the prompt’s values, and writes the value it gives each term to term_assignments_qwen3.5-122b.csv:

A term takes a Practice value or a factor from the list in step 1 when its meaning matches, judged by meaning and not by the words the term contains.
MeSH headings are judged by their NLM scope note.
A term that matches no PCC part, such as “Humans” or “Surveys and Questionnaires”, takes none and is left out of terms.csv.

Syntax: each normalised term gets one written form per database, in term_syntax.csv: phrases in double quotes, truncation with *, and the search field below.

PubMed: recorded, author keyword and OpenAlex keyword terms in [tiab]. MeSH terms in [mh:noexp], which leaves out narrower headings.
Scopus: recorded, author keyword and OpenAlex keyword terms in TITLE-ABS-KEY.
Web of Science: recorded, author keyword and OpenAlex keyword terms in TS.

Selection:

Sharing and reuse: every term that names data (contains data, as in dataset or database), and every MeSH heading, goes to step 3, which selects by database retrieval and load. The Concept is the sharing and reuse of research data, and a term such as “use” or “sharing” alone searches for any use or sharing, so it would swamp the yield threshold.
Factor themes: run separately for each database. Within each theme, taking terms in descending count, keep each one that matches a development set source no kept term matches. A source counts as matched by a MeSH term only if PubMed lists that heading for it, and by an author keyword only if it carries that keyword. A theme with no kept term takes its terms from screening-guide.qmd.
Fallback: reuse always takes its matching terms from the Candidate terms table on the search strategy page, “data reuse” and “data re-use”, which enter each query without the yield test. Nearly every development set source coded for reuse is also coded for sharing (16 of 17), so a reuse term can only add sources a sharing term doesn’t already reach, and the yield rule can’t judge it; the test set, made of sharing sources, can’t either.
Codes with the term none contribute no terms, nor do codes with a problem from the coding checks.
A recorded term from a source coded both sits under sharing and under reuse.

Output: term_assignments_qwen3.5-122b.csv from indexing.py; term_syntax.csv and terms.csv, built by notebook 00 from reference_codes_qwen3.5-122b.csv, reference_indexing.csv and term_assignments_qwen3.5-122b.csv.

term_assignments_qwen3.5-122b.csv, and term_assignments_qwen3.8-27b.csv from the smaller model: one row per distinct indexing term, with its type, its NLM scope note for MeSH headings, the value the model gave it and that value’s theme, any problem with the reply, and the model file, the llama.cpp build, temperature, seed and date of the run; scripts/launch_rds_llm.sh gives the model file’s revision and checksum.
term_syntax.csv: one row per normalised term per database, with the term, the variants it merges, and its written form.
terms.csv: one row per term per database, with these columns:

term: the normalised phrase or heading, such as secondary use or Information Dissemination.
type: recorded, MeSH, author keyword, OpenAlex keyword or fallback.
database: PubMed, Scopus or Web of Science.
field: the database field the term is searched in, such as [tiab], [mh:noexp], TITLE-ABS-KEY or TS.
PCC part: the PCC part it belongs to.
sources in part: the number of development set sources coded for that PCC part, so the strength of each term choice is visible.
assignment basis: the value from term_assignments_qwen3.5-122b.csv for MeSH headings, author keywords and OpenAlex keywords; recorded for recorded terms; the Candidate terms table for fallback terms.
count: the number of development set sources carrying the term for that PCC part.
sources added: for factor terms, the number of those sources that no term kept before it already matches.
DOIs: the DOIs of the sources in sources added for factor terms, and of the sources carrying the term for sharing and reuse terms.
status: to screening for factor terms; empty for sharing and reuse terms, whose status step 3 writes to term_results.csv.

title: Search development plan
text:
Step 3. Query and testing

Principles for constructing the query:

Simple. The query uses as few terms as possible, and a reader can follow why each is there.
Every term earns its place. A candidate drops out when another retrieves at least as many development set sources eligible apart from year in fewer records.
No term picked to catch one source. Known sources a term would add alone go into the records by hand.
Recall comes from the test set. Coverage is the share of indexed test set sources the query retrieves, measured once the query is chosen.
Factors belong to screening. The query finds sources on the topic; whether they report factors is decided at screening, against screening-guide.qmd.
No limit the eligibility criteria don’t impose. No document type or field filters; the date and language limits follow the Research Protocol. Titles left out by the NOT clause mark sources the criteria exclude.
One method, three databases. The same method runs in PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science, translated to each database’s syntax and tested the same way.

API setup: done once, before the first search, on the analysis server. The commands for items 2 to 4 are under Runs, below.

Register the API keys.

PubMed: at ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, sign in with an NCBI account under zachary.batist@mcgill.ca, open Account Settings, and under API Key Management click Create an API Key. The key raises the E-utilities limit from 3 to 10 requests a second.
Scopus: at dev.elsevier.com, click I want an API Key, sign in with an Elsevier account under zachary.batist@mcgill.ca (creating one if needed), click Create API Key, label it RDS-Review with the website URL https://zackbatist.info/RDS-Review, accept the terms, and copy the key. The key gets full Scopus Search access only from McGill’s network. The Scopus Search API allows 20,000 requests a week, at up to 200 records per request.
Web of Science: at developer.clarivate.com, sign up with zachary.batist@mcgill.ca and verify the account. Under Applications, register an application named RDS-Review, then on the Web of Science Starter API page click Subscribe for it and choose the Free Institutional Member Plan (5 requests a second, 5,000 a day; the Free Trial Plan’s 1 a second and 50 a day are too few). Once Clarivate approves it, which can take up to two days, the key shows on the API page.

Store the keys. Create ~/.rds-review-keys, outside the RDS-Review repo, holding three lines that export NCBI_API_KEY, SCOPUS_API_KEY and WOS_API_KEY. Set its permissions to 600, so only your account can read it, and add a line to ~/.bashrc that sources it, so every new shell has the three variables.
Create the Python environment. Create the virtual environment the RDS-Review README sets out, at ~/.venvs/rds-review, and install requirements.txt, which includes requests, the one package the search scripts add. No sudo is needed.
Test each API. Search each database for one source all three index, Fecher, Friesike and Hebing (2015), doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0118053, by DOI. Each test passes when the database returns exactly one record with that DOI. The same script then runs one known phrase, “data sharing”, in each field tag the plan uses: [tiab], [mh:noexp] (as “Information Dissemination”) and [doi] in PubMed; TITLE-ABS-KEY and DOI() in Scopus; TS and DO in Web of Science. Each tag passes when it returns results without an error, so an unsupported tag fails at setup, not mid-run. The Scopus test also prints the weekly quota remaining from the X-RateLimit-Remaining response header; an authorization error there means the request isn’t coming from McGill’s network.

Database access: PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science searches run through the PubMed E-utilities, the Scopus Search API and the Web of Science Starter API from the analysis server. Each run changes into the RDS-Review folder, runs git pull, activates ~/.venvs/rds-review, and reads your API keys from the environment variables. Searches that include source identifiers send them in batches of 25 and sum the results, since longer lists exceed the APIs’ URL limits. File names carry the database as pubmed, scopus or web-of-science, the names data/raw/search_exports/README.md uses.
Earlier method. The first version of this step chose terms from terms.csv by a yield rule and tested coverage and precision. Its queries returned 8,824, 33,089 and 21,721 records for 2015 to 2025, far more than can be screened, and log.md records why it was replaced (“The final queries are too large, 18 November 2026”). Its files (term_results.csv, query_tests.csv, query_misses.csv, query_runs_<database>.csv, load_<database>.csv, precision_sample_<database>.csv) stay in the repo as a record.
Method. Candidate queries are compared on two measures in each database: the records they return for 2015 to 2025 in English and French, and the development set sources eligible apart from year that they retrieve, checked by DOI or PMID with no date limit. A candidate drops out when another retrieves at least as many of those sources in fewer records. Where candidates survive that rule, the choice between them is a judgment, recorded with its reason in log.md. Counts across the three databases match records on DOI, or on title and year, to estimate the load; bib-dedupe deduplicates the review’s records later.
Runs. The Term evidence section of notebook 00 holds every run, in the order each result led to the next: the sharing terms; factor terms, alone, in combination and within five words of “data sharing”; a form of share near data in the title; document types; titles on computing systems; the test set; the known items on the search strategy page; and title terms for governance mechanisms. Each run is a code cell, marked so that rendering skips it, and each writes its results to data/raw/search-development/; the cell after it shows them.
Test. The test set stays out of every run until the query is chosen, then measures its coverage in each database with a 95% Wilson confidence interval. The known items on the search strategy page give a second test.
Factors belong to screening. The query finds sources on the topic; whether they report factors is decided at screening, against screening-guide.qmd, whose factor themes table follows the coding prompt.
Sources added by hand. Known sources the query misses that meet the eligibility criteria go into the records by hand, as other-hand-added_<date>.ris in data/raw/search_exports/.

title: Analysis
text:
Record identifiers
Each deduplicated record has a record_id. It is a hash of the key of the earliest exported record in its group, so it stays the same when a later search adds records or finds the same records again. This holds only while the earlier exports stay in data/raw/search_exports/. Screening decisions and charted data refer to these identifiers. If a later search joins two groups that were separate, one identifier is retired, and notebook 01 lists the change.

title: Analysis
text:
Checks
Notebooks 02, 03, and 04 stop with an error when the data break a rule, and they write nothing until the problem is fixed. The rules include an unknown record_id, a record with no screening decision, a value outside codebook.yml, an empty required cell, and flow counts that do not add up. Warnings, such as a charted source with no factors, are printed and do not stop the run.

title: Research data sharing: a scoping review (RDS-Review)
text:
RDS-Review maps the factors reported to influence the sharing and reuse of research data, including barriers, facilitators, and governance mechanisms. It centres on health research data and compares it with research data sharing in other fields. It updates the 2019 review of research data sharing by Chawinga and Zinn with scoping review methods.
Its taxonomy of factors will support manual annotation for supervised machine learning in the CITF-emails study.






NoteStatus



Draft protocol. The protocol is not yet registered, and the eligibility criteria and limits can still change. See the Research Protocol.


This website hosts the protocol, the codebook, the search and screening materials, and the notebooks that produce the counts, tables, and PRISMA flow diagram. Everything is tracked at github.com/zackbatist/RDS-Review.

Codebook
The charting form, with each variable and its allowed values

Databases, search strings, dates, counts, and the known-item test

title: Screening guide
text: The guide states how records are screened and how decisions are exported for the analysis notebooks. The criteria come from the protocol and are a draft.

title: Screening guide
text:
Stages

Title and abstract. Each deduplicated record gets one decision, include or exclude. When the title and abstract do not allow a decision, include the record.
Full text. Each included record’s full text is retrieved. A report that cannot be retrieved is counted as not retrieved. Each retrieved report gets one decision, and each exclusion gets one reason from the list below.

Each included report is assigned to a source of evidence. Reports of the same study share one source_id.

title: Screening guide
text:
Criteria
A source is included when all of these hold.

It concerns the sharing or reuse of research data.
It reports factors that influence sharing or reuse, including barriers, facilitators, and governance mechanisms.
It concerns health research (tier 1), or it is a review or synthesis of research in other fields or across fields (tier 2).

A source is excluded when it concerns only public health data, other health systems data, or only clinical care data. The rule for routine or clinical data reused for research is not yet set.

title: Updating a Scoping Review of Research Data Sharing with Machine Learning Methods
text: We are updating the 2019 review of research data sharing (Chawinga and Zinn 2019) with scoping review methods from Cavallaro et al. (2026). The 2019 review matches our focus on research data sharing, which makes it a strong candidate for an update. Where it looks at differences across countries, we look at differences across research domains, with special attention on healthcare. Our method draws on the 2026 protocol, which pairs machine learning screening with automated deduplication, and improves on it in two places: deduplication and seed generation.

title: Updating a Scoping Review of Research Data Sharing with Machine Learning Methods
text:
Frameworks and Tools
We follow the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR) and the Joanna Briggs Institute scoping review (JBI) methodology. Both are standard for scoping reviews, make the work reproducible, and are supported by a broad ecosystem of tools and resources.
For deduplication we use ASySD (also used by Perrier et al. (2017)), that, in contrast with Zotero workflow used by Cavallaro et al. (2026), is scriptable for reproducibility purposes. ASReview uses machine learning to rank records by predicted relevance, leveraging Naive Bayes text classification. It needs a seed sample to initialize the ranking. Cavallaro et al. (2026) select their seed sample ad-hoc from the first 5% of deduplicated records.

title: Updating a Scoping Review of Research Data Sharing with Machine Learning Methods

Search and Seed
All four queries build on Chawinga and Zinn (2019). The base query takes their core term, “research data sharing” (RDS). The three concept queries extend that term with the vocabulary the field uses around it. Each pairs one key term (open data, data governance or open science) with “research data” or “data sharing” using AND, so a record must name both the concept and the data practice in its title or abstract. All four queries cover 2015 to 2025, which brackets the 2019 review and picks up where it left off. Manual annotation of seed sample
Terms from the second block of the prior draft query were implicitly grouped around five themes:

Factors that facilitate

Tools and Frameworks

title: Research Protocol
text:
Background
This review maps the factors reported to influence the sharing of research data in health research, including barriers, facilitators, and governance mechanisms.
This review updates the 2019 review of research data sharing (Chawinga and Zinn 2019) with the scoping review methods of Cavallaro et al. (2026). The 2019 review shares this review’s focus on research data sharing, which makes it a strong candidate for an update. It looks at differences across countries. This review looks at differences across research domains, with special attention on healthcare.
Earlier reviews address parts of this topic. Reviews in health and medical research examine incentives (Rowhani-Farid et al. 2017), principles and norms (Kalkman et al. 2019), and governance mechanisms such as harmonized data access agreements (Saulnier et al. 2019). Reviews in public health examine barriers to public health data sharing but exclude research data sharing (van Panhuis et al. 2014).
This review compares health research data sharing with data sharing in general and in other fields. Beyond health, cross-disciplinary reviews cover what drives and inhibits researchers in sharing and reusing data (Fecher et al. 2015; Zuiderwijk et al. 2020; Perrier et al. 2020).
The taxonomy of factors this review produces serves the CITF-emails study, where it supports manual annotation for supervised machine learning on the emails and identifies factors that the emails cover only in part.

title: Research Protocol
text:
Objective and questions
The objective is to map the factors reported to influence the sharing of research data in health research, and to compare them with the factors reported for other fields and for public health data.

Which factors (barriers, facilitators, and governance mechanisms) are reported to influence the sharing of research data in health research?
How can these factors be organized into a taxonomy suitable for annotating correspondence about data sharing?
How do the factors reported for health research differ from those reported for research in other fields and for public health data?

title: Research Protocol
text:
Methods
The review follows the scoping review framework of Arksey and O’Malley (2005) as refined by Levac et al. (2010) and the JBI guidance (Peters et al. 2020). The method draws on the protocol of Cavallaro et al. (2026), which pairs machine learning screening with automated deduplication. It improves on that protocol in deduplication and seed generation. The review is reported according to PRISMA-ScR (Tricco et al. 2018). The searches are reported according to PRISMA-S (Rethlefsen et al. 2021). The flow diagram adapts the PRISMA 2020 template (Page et al. 2021), with “sources of evidence” in place of “studies”.

Eligibility criteria
The criteria follow the population, concept, and context (PCC) structure that JBI recommends for scoping reviews.







Element
Criterion




Population
No restriction. Sources may concern researchers, data stewards, institutions, or governance bodies.


Concept
Factors that influence the sharing of research data, including barriers, facilitators, and governance mechanisms. Research data are data used for research, whether collected for a study or collected for another purpose and reused for research. Data governance comprises the strategies and tools employed to identify, manage, and disseminate data (Leonelli 2019). In health research, data access governance manages who has access to data, for what purposes, and under what conditions, through data access committees, data access agreements, policies, and monitoring (Shabani et al. 2021).


Context, tier 1
Health research. All source types are eligible.


Context, tier 2
Research in other fields and cross-disciplinary research. All source types are eligible.



Sources are excluded when they concern public health data, health systems data, or clinical care data used only for surveillance, service delivery, or patient care. Sources that concern these data reused for research are eligible. The data_origin variable in the codebook records whether a source concerns data collected for research or data reused for research after collection for surveillance, service delivery, or patient care. Each source is assigned a tier at screening from its field.
Sources that design, build or evaluate a specific system, product or service for sharing data are excluded, such as a blockchain framework, a cloud platform or an encryption scheme. Sources that study why people adopt or resist such a system report factors and are eligible.
The search covers sources published from 2015 to 2025 in English and French, the languages the reviewers read.


Information sources and search
One query runs in Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed. It searches titles for a form of share within five words of data, which matches “data sharing” along with phrasings such as “sharing research data” and “sharing of health data”, in sources published from 2015 to 2025 in English and French. It applies no document type filter, since all source types are eligible. The search strategy page gives the query as written for each database, with the number of records it returns.
Candidate queries were compared on the records they return and on how many known relevant sources they find. The known sources are the sources included in the review by Chawinga and Zinn (2019) that meet this review’s criteria, apart from publication year. Those published from 2007 to 2014 served to compare candidate queries, and those published from 2015 were set aside until the query was chosen, to test it on sources it was not built from. A title search returned a small fraction of the records that a search of titles and abstracts returned and found most of the known sources. Factor terms, such as barriers, incentives, and policies, found few more known sources for many more records. The screening guide lists them for reviewers to apply when they screen. The comparisons also showed that about a third of the records in Scopus and Web of Science report a system, product, or service for sharing data, such as a blockchain framework or a cloud storage scheme, which the eligibility criteria exclude. The query leaves out titles that name blockchain, smart contracts, the Internet of Things, vehicular networks, edge computing, or cloud computing, the words that most often mark such sources. Known sources the query misses are added to the records by hand. Section 4 summarizes the measurements and lists the sources added by hand.


Selection of sources
Records are deduplicated with bib-dedupe (Wagner 2024), which, unlike the Zotero workflow of Cavallaro et al. (2026), runs from a script and makes the step reproducible. The records are then screened on title and abstract in ASReview, and again on full text, against the screening guide. Exclusion reasons are recorded at full text. Counts at every stage feed the flow diagram.
ASReview ranks records by predicted relevance with its default model, ELAS u5, which pairs TF-IDF features with a support vector machine. The ranking starts from a seed sample of 200 records drawn at random, with a fixed random seed, from the deduplicated records. The sample size follows the evaluation of the stopping criterion below (Callaghan and Müller-Hansen 2020). The share of relevant records in the seed sample estimates the share across all records, which indicates how much screening the stopping criterion will require. Cavallaro et al. (2026) select their seed sample ad hoc from the first 5% of deduplicated records.
Two reviewers independently screen the titles and abstracts of all records in the seed sample and resolve disagreements through discussion. The annotated seed sample initializes the ASReview ranking. One reviewer screens the ranked records until the stopping rule applies. Both reviewers then independently screen the full texts of the included records and resolve disagreements through discussion.
Screening in ASReview stops on the statistical criterion of Callaghan and Müller-Hansen (2020), in its ranked form. After each screening session, the decisions are exported in the order they were made, seed sample first, and a hypergeometric test on them checks whether recall has reached a target of 95% at a confidence level of 95%. Screening stops when the test rejects the hypothesis that recall falls below the target. In an evaluation of 15 stopping methods on 81 datasets, this criterion alone never stopped before its recall target (Repke et al. 2026), while fixed stopping rules in ASReview fail to generalize across datasets (Kempny et al. 2026). In its authors’ evaluation, the criterion saved 17% of screening on average, and less where few records are relevant, so screening may cover most of the records. These evaluations draw on systematic reviews, so the criterion’s performance in a scoping review remains untested. Recall counts relevant records, so the criterion cannot show whether the unscreened records report factors that the screened records do not.


Data charting
Each included source is charted once into the form defined in the codebook, with one row for the source and one row for each factor it reports. The form is piloted on a sample of sources and revised before full charting begins.
The review does not appraise the included sources, following JBI guidance for scoping reviews (Peters et al. 2020). It maps the factors that sources report, and its eligible source types share no common appraisal tool.


Synthesis
The review codes factors inductively. The resulting taxonomy is a primary output. Counts by tier, field, source type, and year describe the evidence base, and the factor categories are compared across fields.


Artificial intelligence
No large language model makes or suggests eligibility, charting, or synthesis decisions. ASReview ranks records by predicted relevance, and the reviewers make every screening decision. The analysis reruns from the search exports without invoking any language model.
To estimate the screening workload, the first model in Table 1 also judged two sets of records the search returns, 300 drawn at random and the 489 that “research data management” in titles would add, against the screening guide’s criteria, with a prompt that states them. These judgments estimate workload only. They decide no record’s eligibility and enter neither screening nor charting.
A local large language model coded the sources included in the review by Chawinga and Zinn (2019) to identify those that meet this review’s eligibility criteria, which serve as known relevant sources for testing the query. For each source, it recorded the practice, data origin, field, source type, and reported factors from the title and abstract, with the passage that supports each code, choosing from the values listed in its prompt, which come from the eligibility criteria, the screening guide, and the codebook. Notebook 00 reports the codes and keeps the sources that meet the criteria, apart from publication year, as known sources. The model ran at temperature 0 with a fixed seed, which makes its output repeatable. A smaller model, run with the same prompt and settings, agrees with it on 79% to 100% of the codes for each variable, with Cohen’s kappa from 0.63 to 0.84.

text: This notebook reads every export in data/raw/search_exports/, merges duplicate records, and writes data/processed/deduplicated_records.csv. It also writes the identification counts to data/processed/screening_counts.yaml, which 02 Screening extends. Two audit files show what happened. duplicate_groups.csv lists every exported record with the record_id it was merged into and the reason. possible_duplicates.csv lists pairs that look alike but were not merged.

title: 01 Deduplication
text:
Method
Each export is parsed into title, abstract, authors, year, journal, volume, issue, pages, and DOI. Two records are linked as duplicates in three ways.

They share a normalized DOI. The DOI is lowercased and stripped of any resolver prefix.
They share a normalized title and publication year, when the title has at least 20 characters. The title is reduced to lowercase letters and digits after accents are removed.
bib-dedupe labels them duplicates. It compares authors, title, journal, volume, issue, pages, year, and DOI with fuzzy matching, so it also links records that lack a DOI or differ in punctuation, capitalization, or journal abbreviation. The version used is printed at the end of this page.

Links are transitive. Pairs that bib-dedupe labels “maybe” are not merged. A reviewer settles any pair, merged or not, in data/raw/dedup_decisions.csv, with the columns member_a, member_b, and decision (merge or separate). The member identifiers are in duplicate_groups.csv and possible_duplicates.csv.
From each group, the record with the longest abstract supplies the fields, and any field it lacks is filled from the other records in the group.
The record_id is a hash of the key of the earliest record in the group. Records are ordered by search date, file name, and key. The identifier does not change when a later search adds records or finds the same records again, as long as the earlier exports stay in search_exports/. If a later export links two groups that were separate, the identifier of the earlier group is kept and the other is retired. The notebook lists every identifier that changed since the previous run.

    # 1. Exact keys
    first_with = {}
    for i, r in enumerate(records.itertuples()):

        if r.doi:

        if len(r.tkey) >= MIN_TITLE_CHARS and r.year:
            keys.append(("title-year", r.tkey, r.year))
        for k in keys:
            if k in first_with:
                link(first_with[k], i, k[0])
            else:
                first_with[k] = i

    # 2. bib-dedupe. One process, so the result does not depend on the number of processors.
    maybe_pairs = []
    if len(records) > 1:
        bd_input = pd.DataFrame({
            "ID": [str(i) for i in range(len(records))],
            "ENTRYTYPE": "article",
            "title": records["title"],
            "author": records["authors"].str.replace("; ", " and ", regex=False),
            "year": records["year"],
            "journal": records["journal"],
            "volume": records["volume"],
            "number": records["number"],
            "pages": records["pages"],
            "doi": records["doi"],
            "abstract": records["abstract"],
            "search_set": "",
        })
        prepared = bd.prep(bd_input, verbosity_level=0, cpu=1)
        blocked = bd.block(prepared, verbosity_level=0, cpu=1)
        if len(blocked):
            matched = bd.match(blocked, verbosity_level=0, cpu=1)
            for r in matched.itertuples():
                if r.duplicate_label == "duplicate":
                    link(int(r.ID_1), int(r.ID_2), "bib-dedupe")
                elif r.duplicate_label == "maybe":
                    maybe_pairs.append((min(int(r.ID_1), int(r.ID_2)), max(int(r.ID_1), int(r.ID_2))))

    # 3. Reviewer decisions
    decided = {}
    if DECISIONS.exists():
        dec = pd.read_csv(DECISIONS, dtype=str).fillna("")
        dec.columns = [c.strip().lower() for c in dec.columns]
        absent = [c for c in ("member_a", "member_b", "decision") if c not in dec.columns]
        if absent:
            raise ValueError("dedup_decisions.csv is missing column(s): " + ", ".join(absent))
        dec = dec.apply(lambda s: s.str.strip())
        dec["decision"] = dec["decision"].str.lower()
        errs = []
        for n, r in enumerate(dec.itertuples(), start=2):
            if r.member_a not in position or r.member_b not in position:
                errs.append(f"line {n}: member id not found in the exports")
            elif r.member_a == r.member_b:
                errs.append(f"line {n}: member_a and member_b are the same record")
            elif r.decision not in ("merge", "separate"):
                errs.append(f"line {n}: decision must be merge or separate")
        if errs:
            raise ValueError("dedup_decisions.csv has problems:\n- " + "\n- ".join(errs))

            decided[(min(i, j), max(i, j))] = r.decision
            if r.decision == "merge":

    parent = list(range(len(records)))

    def find(i):
        while parent[i] != i:
            parent[i] = parent[parent[i]]

        return i

    # A group needs a look when records are joined only by fuzzy matching or a reviewer decision

        used.add(earliest["key"])

            "year": pick(g, best, "year"),
            "journal": pick(g, best, "journal"),
            "doi": next((d for d in g["doi"] if d), ""),
            "databases": "; ".join(sorted(set(g["database"]))),
            "blocks": "; ".join(sorted(b for b in set(g["block"]) if b)),
            "first_seen": g["search_date"].min(),
            "n_exports": len(g),
